# Many-to-One Encodings

## Goals
- Quantization & rounding as **many→one** (irreversible).  
- Projection $\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^k$ with $k<d$ loses info.  
- Use pigeonhole & rank intuition.

## Quantization Example
Round to tens: $Q_{10}(x)=10\cdot\lfloor x/10\rfloor$.  
**How many** inputs map to $120$? → The set $\{120,\dots,129\}$ (ten of them).

## Pigeonhole Snapshot
If $|A|>|B|$, any $f:A\to B$ has collisions.  
Quantization bins (finite) vs many possible inputs (more) ⇒ collisions.

## Projection Idea (discrete-math level)
Linear map $P:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^k$, $k<d$.  
$\operatorname{rank}(P)\le k<d$ ⇒ nontrivial null space ⇒ **not one-to-one**.

Example (onto the line $y=x$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$):
$$
P=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\[2pt]1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

## Activity: Loss & Distortion Lab
- **Quantize** 20 numbers to 1 decimal; count collisions; compute mean absolute error.  
- **Project** 8 points onto $y=x$; compare pairwise distances before/after (which shrink the most?).  
- **Thought experiment:** flip the LSB vs MSB of a byte—same bit count, different effect.

## Wrap
Name one irreversible map you used and why it’s irreversible.
